data.title: AI companies' deceptive election ads show why Congress must scrutinize super PACs
data.description:
In many of the hottest races in this year’s midterm elections, data centers and artificial intelligence companies were effectively on the ballot. The AI industry knew how unpopular they have become, with voters across the political spectrum furious at them. So, how then could an unpopular industry pour more than $69 million into campaign ads to boost AI-friendly politicians without having their ads backfire when angry voters find out who’s behind them? Simple: Hide who really paid for the ads behind fake names.  

This was perfectly legal — and perfectly outrageous. 

Following in the footsteps of a slew of other unpopular corporate interests and billionaires before them who knew their names were toxic with voters, the AI industry’s super PAC ads hid their sponsorship behind generically named shell groups like “Defending Our Values,” “Think Big,” “American Mission,” and “Jobs and Democracy.” Almost none of the AI industry’s super PAC ads mentioned data centers or AI at all.

This is not something that favored one side or another; it’s a bipartisan problem. An AI super PAC ad for a Republican candidate featured the phrase “CHAMPION AMERICAN INNOVATION” as he shook hands with firefighters, with no mention of data centers or AI. Another AI super PAC ad for a Democrat running for a House seat praised the candidate as committed to reducing gun violence and supporting law enforcement — no mention of AI. The ads were labeled as paid for by a generically named group, not “paid for by AI companies.”

Voters deserve to know who’s really paying for the ads they see so they can make informed decisions at the ballot box. Access to actionable information is at the heart of a healthy democracy — and the very essence of what the First Amendment was designed to protect. 

Congress must close this deceptive super PAC ad loophole before the 2028 elections. The good news is that a recently introduced bill would do exactly that. Inspired by successful voter-approved campaign disclosure laws in Alaska, Arizona and California that passed with cross-partisan support, the Sunlight on SuperPACs Act recently introduced by Reps. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) and Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.) would enact a simple labeling law requiring all super PAC-funded campaign ads to include the names of their top three donors and how much they donated.  

In the case of the AI-funded super PAC ads, they could still use their shell committees to pay for them, but they would have to let voters know that the top funders of the shell committees are AI companies, executives or billionaires. That would give voters the real-time information they need to be able to evaluate the credibility of the ads by seeing who’s paying for them when they’re seeing the ads. Voters are smart but can’t make informed decisions without information.

Courts have already heard multiple corporate-funded challenges to similar state disclosure laws and upheld them all. While we strongly believe that the Supreme Court in Citizens United v. FEC was deeply mistaken in concluding that the First Amendment required allowing corporations to spend unlimited sums to influence elections, the court did unequivocally affirm the constitutionality of campaign disclosure laws.

The Supreme Court has long recognized as consistent with the First Amendment the people’s “informational interest” in requiring election campaigns to provide voters with information about the funders of election ads. Because donor transparency “enables the electorate to make informed decisions and give proper weight to different speakers and messages,” the court has consistently upheld disclosure laws. We are confident it would uphold a super PAC funders labeling law too.

Putting a true source funding label at the bottom of super PAC ads would not address the obscene amount of money being spent on American politics today or limit the questionable claims corporations and billionaires make in their campaign ads. But the Sunlight on SuperPACs Actwill empower voters to be informed about who’s behind the ads they see. Then voters can evaluate the merits of the ads for themselves. We urge the next Congress to give voters that information and shine sunlight on super PACs.

Jon Golinger is the democracy advocate for Public Citizen. Michael Beckel is Money in Politics Reform director for Issue One.

data.title: 'A Republican will never sniff the White House again' if Texas stays blue: Jesse Watters
data.description:
Fox News anchor Jesse Watters warned that if Republicans cannot return to power in Texas, the GOP may never win the presidency again. 

Watters said during his show on Thursday night that Democrats’ sweeping win in the midterm elections could be a death knell for Republicans’ chances of winning future presidential elections.

Democrats won all statewide elections on the ballot Tuesday, leaving Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) as the only remaining GOP statewide official in the Lone Star state. 

“They seize Texas and are on pace for the biggest midterm landslide since Watergate,” Watters said. “Now, if Texas stays blue, a Republican will never sniff the White House ever again.”

The Fox News personality said Republicans had two years to target Democratic opponents without many clear successes, warning that Democrats won’t “take it easy” on the GOP.

“They want it extinguished. They’re already talking about abolishing the Electoral College, impeaching the president, and executing Elon Musk. Democrat governors now control a majority of states where most of the population lives,” Watters added. 

No Democratic elected official has called for the execution of Musk.

Watters said Democrats’ near-win among White voters this cycle reinforced the Republican struggle. After showing a video of a Texas Democratic lawmaker talking about minority races joining to form a majority voting bloc in America, Watters said after Tuesday — that could work. 

“They’re talking about uniting the minority races against whites. Texas Democrat politicians are declaring a political race war. And they could win, because Republicans nearly lost the white vote Tuesday,” he said. 

“Democrats are on the cusp of winning a majority of whites, Blacks, and Hispanics. Open borders is suicide. The Democrats are about to win a Senate seat in Mississippi. Black guy. That’s like Republicans winning Hawaii,” Watters continued. 

The Fox News host said “a lot” of the blame for the midterm losses can also be pinned on the candidates, specifically Ken Paxton (R-Texas) and Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.). He said the GOP’s loss on Tuesday was not a standard midterm correction. 

“This wasn’t your standard midterm thumping,” Watters said. “When Obama got blown out in 2010 and 2014, those races were close. And he didn’t almost lose the Black vote like Republicans almost lost the White vote.”

data.title: Andrews says she won't be focused on 'retribution tour'
data.description:
South Carolina’s newly elected senator, Annie Andrews (D), said her focus will be on “delivering results” and not a “retribution tour” following her victory in the midterm elections.

In the historically red state of South Carolina, Andrews won a competitive Senate race against Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.), who was picked to succeed her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

Andrews won by more than 4 percentage points and more tahn 90,000 votes, according to nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill. The forecaster narrowly favored Darline Graham ahead of the elections.

“Fighting the administration is not going to lower gas prices and grocery prices. It’s not going to solve the problems that I heard about for the past eighteen months,” Andrews told Fox News during an interview. “So I’m going to be laser-focused on delivering results and not, you know, a retribution tour, because that’s what the people of South Carolina are expecting from me.”

Andrews also said she is willing to work with President Trump “to secure the border, to stop these Medicaid cuts” and to “find a way out of this war.”

“I’m going to walk up to the halls of Congress and do my best to solve as many problems as I can for the people of South Carolina,” she added.

Andrews, a pediatrician, launched her bid to run for a seat in the U.S. Senate last year. She previously ran for office in 2022 against Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), losing by around 14 points. Four years later, she won her Senate bid, becoming the first Democrat to hold a Senate seat from the state in decades.

Andrews’s win is consistent with the Democrats’ nationwide victory in the midterm elections this November, where the party took control of both the Senate and the House. Democrats secured big wins in battleground states, flipping GOP-held seats in places like Texas, Maine, Iowa, Ohio and Michigan.

data.title: Democrats can't heal the US-Canada bond Trump destroyed
data.description:
Democrats won control of both the Senate and House on Tuesday, and Canadians breathed a sigh of relief. After nearly two years of insults, economic coercion, talk of Canada becoming the 51st state, and the whole “Lake America” debacle, their relief is understandable. 

But it would be a mistake to think that Canadians are willing to return to the status quo ante — to the pre-Trump Canada-U.S. relationship. Neither this congressional election nor a change of president in 2028 is likely to restore the bilateral relationship both countries until recently considered normal. 

The international order that gave rise to that relationship is dying. It took shape and flourished within a system structured around American power: first during the Cold War’s bipolar confrontation, then during the unipolar era following the Soviet Union’s collapse. In both periods, U.S. leadership underpinned unusually close economic, political and security ties. 

For Canada, the benefits were substantial. During the Cold War, American strategic power helped secure Canada against the Soviet threat, while Ottawa and Washington developed an increasingly integrated system of continental defense.

After 1991, American dominance allowed Canada to scale back defense spending and helped sustain an open international economy in which it prospered through continental trade and multilateral cooperation. That security and prosperity also created space for Ottawa to punch above its weight as a constructive middle power. 

The arrangement was never free of friction, but its underlying logic was clear: Close integration with the U.S. made economic and strategic sense. Ironically, by enabling Ottawa to play an outsized role as a helpful fixer and respected peacekeeper, that integration also allowed Canada to be more distinctively Canadian. 

Today, that order is giving way to a more fragmented multipolar world, characterized by renewed great-power competition and the erosion of the architecture of international cooperation. Prime Minister Mark Carney captured this shift at Davos in January when he declared that “the old order is not coming back.”

His point was not simply that Canada could no longer count on an America governed by Trump. The foundations of Canadian foreign, economic and security policy were undergoing an epochal transformation.

Multipolarity complicates Canada’s traditional calculation because it changes the incentive structure in Washington. Confronted by China’s rising power, Russia’s challenge to European security and the erosion of American primacy, the U.S. is reevaluating global commitments, pressing allies to shoulder more burdens, onshoring industrial capacity and treating trade and technology as instruments of strategic competition. 

Where Washington once had greater latitude to sustain an open economy and tolerate differences with allies, it now increasingly judges close partnerships by their contribution to strategic priorities. For Canada, dependence on American power consequently carries risks that were less pronounced in the past. 

Trump has pursued this adjustment in an especially undiplomatic and confrontational fashion. His tariffs and threats against Canada have made the risks of dependence painfully clear. Yet the broader American shift toward strategic competition, economic nationalism and selective international engagement is not simply a product of Trump’s preferences. It reflects structural realities that will persist long after he leaves office. 

That is why Tuesday’s election, whatever relief it brings, will not derail or even significantly delay Canada’s ongoing strategic realignment. Congress can challenge tariffs and encourage a more cooperative bilateral relationship. A post-Trump White House may restore a measure of civility and predictability. And all of that will matter. But neither Democrats nor Republicans can recreate the international order that once made Canadian-American economic integration and strategic alignment seem both natural and optimal. 

For Ottawa, the logical response is greater strategic autonomy — not separation from the United States, but the capacity to make more choices without being unduly constrained by Washington. 

Geography and history make total rupture unrealistic. The two countries share deeply integrated supply chains, vital infrastructure and a continent whose defense requires close cooperation. Russian and Chinese capabilities, the strategic importance of the Arctic and the intensification of gray-zone competition make that cooperation more necessary, not less. The American market will likewise remain indispensable to Canadian prosperity. 

Strategic autonomy must operate within those constraints. The objective is not some sort of fortress Canada or a profound rupture of the Canada-U.S. relationship. Rather, in keeping with Prime Minister Carney’s strategy of “value-based realism,” the goal is to diversify trade where practical, strengthen Canadian defense-industrial capacity, build sovereign capabilities and enhance partnerships in Europe and the Indo-Pacific. These are means of increasing Ottawa’s freedom of action.  

Tuesday’s election may make the Canada-U.S. relationship less contentious, but it cannot reverse the overall trajectory of that relationship. Canada and the U.S. are both adapting to the emergence of a new geopolitical ecosystem — one which is generating new interests, incentives and anxieties in both capitals. 

For Ottawa, greater strategic autonomy was never merely a response to Trump. It is a rational adaptation to this new ecosystem. Whoever governs in Washington, that reality is not going away. 

Andrew Latham is a professor of international relations at Macalester College in Saint Paul, Minn., a senior fellow at the Institute for Peace and Diplomacy, and a non-resident fellow at Defense Priorities in Washington.

data.title: Waters launches bid for House Financial Services chair
data.description:
Democratic Rep. Maxine Waters (Calif.) officially launched her bid for chair of the House Financial Services Committee on Friday, after Democrats won control of the lower chamber in the midterms. 

In a letter to her Democratic colleagues, Waters — the committee’s ranking member — wrote that party lawmakers “must now deliver on our promises to the American people” and lower the cost of living. Democrats on the campaign trail vowed to ease prices, as gas and grocery costs have risen this year amid the Iran war. 

Referencing the “affordability crisis” facing Americans, the California lawmaker blasted the Trump administration for “dismantling consumer safeguards, eliminating access to safe and affordable housing” and engaging in what she described as “unprecedented levels of corruption.”

Given that, Waters wrote it “has never been more important to have a proven, effective and innovative leader” at the helm of the Financial Services panel.

“I am that leader,” she argued in her letter, which a Waters spokesperson shared with The Hill. 

Waters, 88, chaired the committee from 2019 to 2023, when Democrats last controlled the House. She has led Democrats on the panel since 2013. 

Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.), who has helmed the committee since January 2025, narrowly won his reelection bid over Democrat Chris Jones.

Waters is not the only Democrat vying for the Financial Services gavel. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) launched his bid for chair on Thursday, writing in a letter to his Democratic colleagues the panel must address homeownership, frauds and scams and President Trump’s approach to white-collar crime, among other issues. 

Waters also laid out her planned agenda on Friday. The California Democrat vowed to pursue a “bold agenda,” writing she will build on the bipartisan housing law that took effect over the summer, crack down on junk fees and “permanently and independently fund” the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

The Trump administration has sought to dismantle the agency, which is an independent entity within the Federal Reserve.

As for the cryptocurrency industry, Water wrote she will “stop” the Trump family’s “crypto corruption” while establishing “tough but fair rules of the raid for legitimate crypto ventures.”

The California Democrat later proposed tweaking logistical elements of the panel, including by renaming it the “Committee on Housing and Financial Services” to put “housing first.”

She also said she will discuss “ways to empower Subcommittee chairs” with her colleagues and create three new positions: a committee whip role occupied by a junior member, a freshman representative and a committee messenger.

data.title: Sununu blames Trump for GOP midterm shellacking
data.description:
Senate Republican candidate John Sununu says President Trump deserves much of the blame for Republicans’ blowout losses in Tuesday’s election, which will give Democrats their biggest Senate and House majorities in years.

Sununu in an interview with SiriusXM’s “The John Kasich Show” said Trump’s inability to end the months-long conflict with Iran and his failure to “drain the swamp” as he pledged to do in the 2024 campaign cost Republican candidates dearly.

“Now it seems like he or his family is on every transaction and deal that goes on in Washington,” Sununu said. “Those two things, I think, caused people to say, ‘You know, I just can’t vote for a Republican while he’s still in office.'”

Sununu lost the New Hampshire Senate race to Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) by 13 percentage points despite Republican hopes that they had a good chance of stealing the Democratic-held seat. 

Sununu represented New Hampshire in the U.S. Senate from 2003 to 2009, when he was defeated by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.)

Trump, however, has blamed GOP candidates for not doing a good enough job of promoting themselves and has argued that he would have carried many of them to victory if he were on the ballot as he was two years ago.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump posted on Truth Social on Tuesday night as the election returns showed a blue wave sweeping across the country.

Vice President Vance on Wednesday cited the war with Iran as the biggest reason why Republicans fared so poorly in this year’s midterm election.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a social media post.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance argued.  

“But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” he said.

But some Republican strategists are acknowledging privately that Democrats’ attacks on Trump’s family business dealings and other allegations of corruption in the Trump administration also moved voters.

Sununu told “The John Kasich Show” that future Republican presidential aspirants such as Vance will suffer political fallout after Republicans’ disastrous showing in the midterms.

“The closer you are to the president, the worse a night it was for you as a potential presidential candidate,” he said.

Sununu predicted that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) would explore a presidential run in the next election cycle to boost her political brand.

“Some people run for president because they really think they can win and that they’ll be a great leader and an important leader for the country. Some people run for president because it’s good for their business model,” he said.

“And I put AOC in the latter category. So, will she test the waters and go through the kabuki? 100 percent. Because her business model is built around followers and attention,” he added.

data.title: Democrats win big after Trump alienates voters
data.description:
President Trump told Americans to vote as if he were on the ballot. They did. And now a lot of Republicans probably wish the president had never opened his mouth.

It wasn’t a blue wave — it was a blue earthquake, as the New York Times put it. It’s not easy to lose both houses of Congress — but thanks to the president, Republicans managed to do just that. 

Two years ago Trump told voters that when he’s elected president, inflation would come down. It’s higher today than when Joe Biden left office. He promised lower food prices. Anybody who’s been to a supermarket lately knows how that worked out. He said the war with Iran would last a few weeks. Wrong again.

A recent NBC News poll finds that 71 percent of Americans think we’re on the wrong track. You’d think a number like that might have persuaded the president to spend the closing days of the campaign talking about grocery bills.

But Trump had a few other things on his mind. He spoke about his fascination with the rear ends of a Republican senator and singer Nicki Minaj.

The day before Election Day, in his final public speech, he went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and spoke for more than 20 minutes about gravel, new grass, pipes and algae.

A week earlier he told a rally that “Norway sucks” because the folks there who hand out the Nobel Peace Prize neglected to give him one.

He called Bill Maher “a complete and total loser” because Maher apparently didn’t give the president the respect he thinks he deserves.

Imagine being a Republican candidate in a close race, hoping the president might say a few words about the cost of living, but instead you get his musings about algae, Norway, Bill Maher and rear ends.

Make no mistake, Republicans got what they deserved. For two years they said virtually nothing about tariffs or the war or those inexcusable pardons on his first day in office of the rioters at the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 — or anything else Trump said or did that hurt the party. Not in public, anyway. In private they knew what everybody else knew — that the president was in way over his head … on the war, on inflation, on affordability, which he recklessly called a “hoax.”

He never told the voters that he understood their pain. He couldn’t. Because he has no empathy.     

His Republican allies may think they were being loyal to their leader, but it was shameless cowardice dressed up as loyalty. Sycophancy comes with a price — a price Republicans are now paying.

In the world of politics, there is nothing especially remarkable about a president hurting his enemies. It takes a special talent to do this much damage to your friends.

But in spite of everything, Trump did have a legitimate case to make against the Democrats. When he told voters that the party’s left wing wanted to usher in a socialist America, he could point to progressives whose wish-list includes a national wealth tax, Medicare for all, abolishment of ICE, abandonment of Israel — and that’s for openers. Some progressives would go further and move for a federal takeover of some corporations. The Democratic Socialists of America want to defund the police and shut down prisons. They have no use for capitalism and aren’t afraid to say so.

And yet, in spite of all that, the Democrats won, because it wasn’t only Trump’s policies that voters rejected — it was Trump himself. They rejected his vulgarity, his out-of-control narcissism, his unlimited appetite for vengeance.

And the worst of Trump rubbed off on the president’s allies, who somehow figured that nastiness might be the path to victory.

In Kansas, incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R) accused his Democratic opponent of “probably grooming” children. Marshall lost.

In Texas, Republicans insinuated that Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is gay. Talarico won.

And President Trump called Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a “vicious, violent jihadist.” El-Sayed won.

So did Democratic Senate candidates in Maine, Iowa, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina — and before it’s over, maybe a few more states.

As impressive as the Democratic victory was, it was hardly a mandate for them to do a lot of things nobody voted for. Do Americans really want Trump impeached for a third time? Progressives might, but they don’t represent Middle America. Do Americans really want non-stop investigations of Trump and anybody that got close to him during the past two years? Do they want the socialist wing of the party to run roughshod over more moderate Democrats?

If Democrats don’t bring down prices and give Americans hope that we’re heading in the right direction, in two years they may very well be where Republicans are now: devastated and disheartened, on the outside looking in.

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page.

data.title: 'Voter apathy' toward Hyde-Smith could be factor in Mississippi Senate race: Professor
data.description:
A Mississippi political science professor said voters seemed to be “really enthusiastic” about Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom, but when it comes to his opponent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), “there was a lot of voter apathy.”

“Colom’s a really high-quality candidate,” said Aaron Hitefield, assistant professor in the Department of Political Science and Public Administration at Mississippi State University, during an appearance on NewsNation.

“Voters seemed really enthusiastic about him … when you compare that to Cindy Hyde-Smith, the current incumbent, there was a lot of voter apathy,” Hitefield added. “I think you see that in the results currently.”

The Senate race in the historically red-leaning state remains uncalled days as Colom maintains a lead of a little over 2,000 votes, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ. In the neck-to-neck battle for a seat in the U.S. Senate, Democrat is leading by just 0.2 percentage.

The chair of the Mississippi Republican Party, Mike Hurst, told the press Thursday that if “the laws are followed and the voters spoke, that is it and Mississippi Republicans will accept that.”

“There is no election denying going on here,” he said.

The ballots are still being received in the Magnolia State, which allows mail ballots to be counted and received up to five business days after the election as long as they are postmarked by Election Day.

Attorneys for Hyde-Smith recently demanded in a letter sent to the election commissioners in all 82 Mississippi counties, that election officials separate the affidavit ballots, document their disposition and preserve “all associated materials.”

An attorney for Colom, in a letter sent to county election commissioners Thursday, said the Republicans’ demands “have no basis in Mississippi law.”

“If you depart from ordinary election procedures as you have been asked to do, you will violate Mississippi voters’ rights and Mississippi election law,” the lawyer wrote in the letter.

By current tally, the Democrats will hold 54 Senate seats and, with Mississippi and Alaska still undecided, that number could grow to 56.

data.title: Was the midterm outcome a rebuke or a reach across the aisle?
data.description:
With apologies to Cole Porter, was the election a rebuke or merely an invitation to compromise? 

Although President Trump saw it as an invitation, he asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot, and they did. If it looks like a rebuke, walks like a rebuke and talks like a rebuke, it’s a rebuke. Americans voted, and they voted no to Trump. 

Money hardly availed the Republicans. Trump’s offer of $5,000 to every American if Republicans retained congressional control fell on deaf ears. Even money from Trump’s lapdog Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, who wasted hundreds of millions of dollars to sway voters to the Republican side, had zero impact on the outcome. 

The vote was a stunning upset victory for American democracy. There were no reports of violence at the polls. The Proud Boys stayed home. There were no stories of voter intimidation, no allegations of widespread fraud or false certification. The margins of victory were in almost all cases decisive. There was just no room for shenanigans. 

Democrats flipped seven seats to win a majority in the Senate, including previously held Republican strongholds that Trump won by double digits in 2024, notably Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. They will win at least 259 House seats, well beyond the 218 needed to secure a majority, an NBC News analysis shows. 

Democrats also broke into critical areas where they had long languished like lions in the veld, including Florida and possibly Mississippi, which are essential to building a durable governing coalition.  

Trump conceded it was a landslide and blamed the Iran war for the trouncing. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he will not even run for minority leader in the new Congress.

The clear message to Washington read loud and clear, and it was overwhelming. Get things done. Make the administration accountable for its unprecedented corruption and baffling foreign policy. End the war in Iran on favorable terms. Throw the rascals out! Whatever is going on is not what we want. 

The policy agendas of Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, a primary creator of Project 2025, and White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller, enforcer of the sadistic mass deportation programs that smacked of the Nazi era, were voted anathema to the American people.  

Finally, despite all the propaganda about communists lurking under the Democratic bed, the elections produced a diverse team of fresh Democratic voices: a pro-Palestinian Muslim, women, citizens who had never held public office and the first openly gay man elected to the United States Senate. All attuned to the issues that concern younger generations, who refuse to be stratified by shopworn political shibboleths. 

The tortuous road to the flat-out Democratic victory ran through a number of key milestones. Those included selecting smart, savvy candidates who could win in different parts of the country, responding aggressively to the Republican mid-decade gerrymander and then flipping the very seats that the Republicans had redrawn, bitterly fought court victories and the hard work of pro-democracy groups to ensure that the administration’s efforts to discredit the election never got off the ground. 

Federal district judges, even at the risk of physical threats, played a key role by throttling unconstitutional White House efforts to seize state voting records, curtail mail-in voting and manipulate the count in Alaska.  

“We the people” has been the driver behind our finest hours. The tragedies in Minneapolis galvanized the nation and showed how to fight for a different kind of American story than the nihilism Republicans offered.            

So, who were the real winners besides Minority Leaders Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.)? True, the American people were spared a potential constitutional crisis, and the perfect storm of a MAGA White House and a supine Congress is over. 

But there are still barriers to ultimate success. Democrats must not waste time pressing impeachments, open borders, wealth taxes or even Supreme Court reform as much as it is needed. Instead, they must land on such policies as healthcare, trade, immigration, artificial intelligence regulation, trimming the national debt at the moment surpassing $40 trillion. You choose the order. 

And, as Churchill said, “In Victory, Magnanimity.” Democrats must be ready to make common cause with Republicans, no longer fearful of Trump, to make sensible policies that are veto proof. And be mindful of the Supreme Court. Pundits are discussing the idea of Alito retiring, which would give Trump the chance to ram through a young Alito doppelganger. The new Congress will not be seated until January. 

The Republicans will have many challenges as well. With Trump as a lame duck in his last two years in office, can they repudiate the policies of incompetent ideologues such as Hegseth, Miller and Vought, returning like Odysseus to the center-right party of Ronald Reagan? Free markets, small government, low taxes and a sensible bipartisan foreign policy that seeks stability in the Middle East and punishes authoritarians who would project power beyond their borders? 

As Richard Haass has said, “The country has dodged a bullet, but it is not out of the woods.” 

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

data.title: Republican wipeout: Trump created too many problems for himself and his party
data.description:
What was expected to be a strong showing for the Democrats turned out to be a total wipeout of the Republican Party as we know it. The Democrats made massive gains in the House and the Senate. It was the kind of devastating outcome for Republicans that we haven’t seen in a while, the likes of which it doesn’t just take a single election cycle to reverse.

Nearly every group that shifted toward Republicans in 2024 shifted back in 2026. So what happened? 

It’s very simple: It was a cost-of-living election. Democrats were laser-focused on promising to address the cost of living crisis, whereas President Trump was laser-focused on … his ballroom. He was taking dinners with tech oligarchs. He was bragging about the stock market and oil profits — in other words, about how rich everyone except you is getting at the top. 

Exit polls showed that the skyrocketing cost of living and government corruption were the top concerns of voters. Their lives have become unaffordable due to the exploding cost of housing, health care, education, insurance, utilities, and of course, groceries and gas. 

Many voted for Trump in 2024 because they remembered the 2019 economy — when they had a little bit more money in their pockets at the end of the month.

That’s no longer so. Inflation has been outpacing wage growth for much of this year. So when Trump touted the “Golden Age of America” in rally after campaign rally, it wasn’t a rallying cry to the winners of a blazing hot economy — it was a finger in the eye of the losers in an economy whose vitality is based on tech speculation and the high gas prices that are killing consumers. 

The constant reporting about extreme corruption at the highest levels of the Trump administration only added insult to injury. Former White House budget director and Trump chief of staff Mick Mulvaney appeared on my NewsNation show a few weeks ago. Reflecting on a poll that showed corruption as the top issue for 88 percent of voters, he remarked, “What people are telling the president is, ‘Look, we’re tired of you getting rich and us getting poor.'” 

The Democrats’ analysis of their good fortune Tuesday night is spot on: Trump told people to vote like he was on the ballot, and they did.

But on the right, another singular explanation has emerged to explain the disaster we all witnessed unfold: the war in Iran, which was the third most important factor voters gave in exit polls explaining their vote. 

Certainly, gas prices surged after the attack and still remain high. But as the exit polls show, the war in Iran was one of many things voters were upset about. And the thing that upset them about the war in Iran was not the attack itself, which was at least initially popular with Republican voters in many polls throughout March and even April. It was the fact that the war just kept going without any signs of a conclusion, becoming one more thing making their lives harder and more unaffordable. 

A timeline of Trump’s approval ratings makes clear that although the war in Iran resulted in a steep dropoff, his approval really started to slip long before that — after the Liberation Day tariffs of April 2025. His approval rating has never recovered from that.

I believe that Trump and his party could have survived any one of these problems, but not all three. If the cost of housing and health care and groceries were coming down, a dollar more per gallon at the pump would have been more tolerable. If Trump had not spent so much time talking up the ballroom and other expensive vanity projects, voters might have had more patience with the tariffs.

If voters felt like they were making money, they might have minded less that everyone in the president’s orbit seems to be making billions off the presidency, some of them through dodgy cryptocurrency schemes.

It was everything together that revealed a presidency simply unable to focus on the main promises of his campaign in 2024. Those promises were fourfold: Radically reduce immigration; bring costs down and get money back in the pockets of working Americans; drain the swamp; and no new wars. He succeeded at only one, failing rather ostentatiously at all the others.
